doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: Making a living: studio and odd work
title: How jazz musicians really make a living
summary: Great gigs are highlights, so he filled the rest of his time with varied work, often saying yes and learning on the job.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: No. Those things are great. And that’s what — people I don’t think have a realistic picture of what jazz musicians, or a lot of musicians, how they really make a living. That playing with Ella and the list of people you’ve played with, Zoot Sims and Sweets Edison, those are great moments, and you’re recording here, but that doesn’t happen every single day.

No. Those are the highlights and high points. But unless you maybe were touring for long periods with a Stan Getz, or — like for instance I worked with Stan in different venues, concert situations, but never to tour, for like six months or whatever. So yeah, you have to fill up the rest of your time with other stuff, and so I’ve done a lot of stuff. I said to somebody recently, I’ve done just about everything except maybe play in a circus band, because they didn’t use keyboards then, now they do. But a lot of it has just been kind of I guess daring or something. I never thought of it that way, but I used to, again kind of in keeping with what we were talking about, I would, like with a lot of studio work, I would just say yes, and hope that I could pull it off, and a lot of it was just on the job training. If I’d had more sense I guess I would have said I’d better pass on this, I don’t think I can do it. And you just get in there and you figure out how to do it because you’re expected to, and you’re going to look pretty stupid if you can’t.
